answer.decision: Adopt tail-aware sampling that retains all error traces and very slow requests while randomly sampling normal successful traffic at a lower rate.
answer.action: Deploy the prototype tail sampler using rules that retain 100% of error traces and requests above the p99 latency threshold, plus a calibrated random sample of normal traffic; validate at least a 40% cost reduction and sufficient per-service sample sizes for latency analysis before full rollout.
reasons: The prototype reduced stored trace volume by 55%, exceeding the required 40% reduction, while retaining all injected error and p99 traces.
Errors are rare but highly valuable: 0.7% of requests provide 46% of traces used in incident reviews.
Normal successful traffic exceeds 98% of volume, so reducing its retention produces substantial savings with less diagnostic impact.
Independent, fully aggregated metrics preserve broad service-level latency measurement, while sampled normal traces support detailed latency analysis.
The backend supports retention decisions after spans are assembled, making tail-aware selection feasible.
assumptions: The prototype's 55% storage reduction is representative of production traffic and translates sufficiently to telemetry cost.
The normal-traffic sampling rate will be set per service or volume tier to maintain statistically useful latency samples.
The p99 threshold and error classification are available and reliable when tail-sampling decisions are made.
risks: Low-volume services may retain too few normal traces for reliable trace-level latency analysis unless minimum sample floors are applied.
Tail sampling may increase buffering, processing latency, and sampler resource consumption.
Incorrect thresholds, incomplete traces, or sampler failures could cause valuable traces to be dropped.
A 55% reduction in stored volume may not yield an equal bill reduction if fixed or ingestion-related charges dominate.

citations.claim: The prototype tail sampler reduced stored trace volume by 55% and retained all injected error and p99 test traces.
Errors are 0.7% of requests but account for 46% of traces used during incident reviews.
Requests above p99 are 1% of volume, while normal successful traffic exceeds 98%.
Metrics are independently collected at full aggregation and do not require retaining every trace.
The backend supports tail-based retention decisions after spans are assembled.
